title: An Octopus Has Busy Arms
text: An octopus has eight flexible arms. Each arm has rows of suckers that can taste and touch. An octopus also has three hearts. It can squeeze through a small gap because it has no hard bones. That is one clever ocean animal!
context: A short introduction to octopus bodies.
vocabulary: flexible: able to bend easily
suckers: round gripping parts on an arm
source: Original summary of Smithsonian Ocean animal information

title: A Bee Dances a Map
text: A honey bee can tell other bees where to find flowers. Back at the hive, it moves in a waggle dance. The turns and wiggles give clues about direction and distance. The tiny dancer helps the whole group find a good meal.
context: A simple explanation of the honey bee waggle dance.
vocabulary: hive: the home of a bee group
direction: the way something is located
source: Original summary of USDA honey bee information

references.citation: United States Department of Agriculture, honey bee waggle dance educational materials

title: A Penguin's Warm Coat
text: Penguins do not wear fuzzy sweaters. Their own feathers make a warm coat. Many small feathers overlap and help block cold water. Penguins also have a layer of fat. Some penguins stand close together when the air is bitterly cold.
context: A young-reader explanation of penguin insulation.
vocabulary: overlap: partly cover one another
layer: one thickness of material
source: Original summary of British Antarctic Survey penguin information

title: An Elephant's Amazing Trunk
text: An elephant uses its trunk in many ways. It can smell, breathe, drink, pick up food, and spray water. The trunk can lift a heavy branch or gently touch a small object. It is a nose and a powerful tool together.
context: An introduction to the many jobs of an elephant's trunk.
vocabulary: trunk: the long nose of an elephant
source: Original summary of Smithsonian's National Zoo elephant information

title: A Sea Otter Uses a Rock
text: A sea otter may use a rock as a tool. Floating on its back, the otter can tap a hard shell against the rock. When the shell opens, lunch is ready. Some otters even keep a favorite rock for later.
objectives: practice the letters t and o
context: A simple example of tool use by sea otters.
vocabulary: tool: an object used to do a job
source: Original summary of Monterey Bay Aquarium sea otter information

title: The Owl's Quiet Flight
text: Many owls have special edges on their wing feathers. These edges help soften the sound of moving air. Quiet flight can help an owl listen while it flies. The owl is not truly silent, but its feathery design keeps the noise low.
objectives: learn how owl feathers help flight
context: A short explanation of quiet owl flight.
vocabulary: edge: the outside line of something
design: the way parts are arranged
source: Original summary of Smithsonian bird information

references.citation: Smithsonian, educational information about owl feathers and flight

title: How a Frog Gets a Drink
text: A frog does not need to sip water like a person. It can take in water through a special patch of skin on its belly and legs. Frogs need clean, damp places because their thin skin is important for water and air.
objectives: practice the letters f and r
context: A simple explanation of how frogs absorb water.
vocabulary: damp: a little wet
absorb: take in
source: Original summary of U.S. Geological Survey amphibian information

references.citation: U.S. Geological Survey, Amphibian Research and Monitoring Initiative

title: A Dolphin's Special Whistle
text: A bottlenose dolphin can develop its own special whistle. Other dolphins may learn that sound and use it to get the dolphin's attention. Scientists call it a signature whistle. It works a little like a name carried through the water.
context: An introduction to signature whistles in bottlenose dolphins.
vocabulary: signature: a special identifying mark or sound
source: Original summary of NOAA dolphin research

references.citation: NOAA Fisheries, bottlenose dolphin communication research

title: The Red Panda's Extra Grip
text: A red panda has a wrist bone that sticks out like an extra thumb. This false thumb helps the animal grip bamboo while it eats. Red pandas also use sharp claws for climbing. Their useful paws are built for life among trees.
context: A young-reader look at a red panda adaptation.
vocabulary: bamboo: a tall, woody grass
grip: hold tightly
source: Original summary of Smithsonian's National Zoo red panda information

title: A Turtle Carries Its Ribs
text: A turtle's shell is not a house that it can leave. The shell is part of its skeleton. Its ribs and backbone connect to the hard shell. A turtle carries this strong body armor everywhere, even when it rests or swims.
objectives: learn what a turtle shell is
practice the letters t and l
context: A basic anatomy fact about turtle shells.
vocabulary: skeleton: the bones inside a body
armor: a hard protective covering
source: Original summary of Smithsonian animal information

references.citation: Smithsonian, educational information about turtle shells

title: The Capybara Takes a Swim
text: A capybara is the world's largest rodent. It has slightly webbed feet and lives near rivers, ponds, or marshes. Its eyes, ears, and nose sit high on its head. The capybara can watch and breathe while most of its round body stays underwater.
context: A young-reader introduction to a swimming rodent.
vocabulary: rodent: a mammal with front teeth that keep growing
webbed: joined by skin between the toes
source: Original summary of San Diego Zoo capybara information

title: The Axolotl Stays Young
text: An axolotl is a salamander that keeps its feathery gills as an adult. It spends its whole life in water. An axolotl can regrow a lost leg and other body parts. Wild axolotls are in serious danger, so people are working to protect their watery home in Mexico.
context: A simple look at an unusual salamander and its conservation.
vocabulary: gills: body parts used to breathe in water
regrow: grow again
source: Original summary of Aquarium of the Pacific axolotl information

title: A Tiny Garden in Sloth Fur
text: A sloth's coarse hairs have tiny grooves. In the damp forest, algae can grow in those grooves and give the fur a green tint. Moths and beetles may live there too. The sloth carries a small ecosystem while it hangs quietly among green leaves.
context: A young-reader explanation of the living community in sloth fur.
vocabulary: algae: simple living things that often grow in water
ecosystem: living things and their surroundings
source: Original summary of Smithsonian's National Zoo sloth information

title: The Meerkat on Lookout
text: Meerkats live together in groups called mobs. While others eat, dig, or rest, one meerkat may stand guard. The sentry rises on its back legs and scans for danger. Group members take turns watching, so one small animal is not always stuck with lookout duty.
context: A simple explanation of sentry duty in a meerkat group.
vocabulary: sentry: someone who watches for danger
mob: a group of meerkats
source: Original summary of Smithsonian's National Zoo meerkat information

title: The Mole-Rat Digging Team
text: Naked mole-rats dig tunnels as a team. The animal in front bites into hard soil. Workers behind it sweep the loose dirt backward. The last worker kicks the dirt outside. Their lips close behind their big front teeth, so they can dig without filling their mouths with soil.
context: A young-reader description of naked mole-rat teamwork.
vocabulary: tunnel: a passage under the ground
worker: a group member that performs a task
source: Original summary of Smithsonian's National Zoo naked mole-rat information
